TranscriptSegments.Content: What was it like to ask for prioritization in the meeting?
I almost did not do it.
My heart was racing before I spoke, but I said, I can move both cases forward, and I need help deciding which one takes precedence today.
My supervisor looked at the list and said the same thing I had been hoping she would say.
One of them could wait.
What did you notice after she said that?
Relief first, then embarrassment.
I had spent 2 days acting like both things were life or death, and it turned out there was a reasonable answer.
The embarrassment is understandable.
Can it also be information that your internal alarm is louder than the actual situation sometimes?
I think so.
I keep expecting people to be irritated when I need something, and then they are usually just practical.
What did you do with the time that opened up?
I finished the urgent case, left work before 7, and had dinner with Nora.
Not a perfect evening.
I checked my phone twice.
But I did not open my laptop.
How did Nora respond to the conversation you planned to have?
Better than I expected.
I told her that when I get stressed, I act like I want space, even when I actually need someone nearby.
She said she can ask whether I want company or quiet instead of guessing.
That sounds like a clear request from both of you.
It felt vulnerable.
I am used to trying to make my needs invisible, so nobody has to accommodate me.
What is the cost of making them invisible?
People cannot meet them.
Then I feel lonely and resentful, even though I never told anyone what was happening.
That is an important pattern to notice.
How does it show up outside of work and home?
With my sister.
She calls and asks how I am, and I always say I am fine because she has her own life.
Then I feel sad that she does not know what is going on with me.
Would there be a middle ground between telling her nothing and asking her to carry everything?
Maybe I could tell her I have been having a difficult stretch and that I do not need her to fix it.
I could just ask if she has time to talk this weekend.
That sounds direct and kind to both of you.
I do not know why directness feels so much harder than being overwhelmed in private.
Private overwhelm may feel more familiar.
Directness introduces uncertainty, but it also gives people an opportunity to respond to the real situation.
I keep thinking about my dad.
He did not like asking for help either.
Toward the end, he would say he was fine when he was clearly uncomfortable.
I hated not knowing what he needed.
That memory may be helping you see the pattern from another angle.
Yes, I do not want Nora or my sister to have to guess.
I also do not want to become someone who only reaches out when things are unbearable.
What would a smaller reaching out practice look like?
I can text my sister tonight and ask if she has time for a call this weekend.
I can tell her it has been a difficult month without making it sound like an emergency.
That is a good example of a clear bounded request.
The darker thoughts have been quieter this week.
I still had one anxious night, but I did not feel like disappearing.
I made tea, sat with Nora, and went to bed.
Do you have any plan or intention to harm yourself today?
No, I do not.
Good.
We will keep checking in while also making room for the rest of what you are working on.
What would you like to practice before next time?
The call with my sister.
And I want to keep asking the priority question at work when I need it.
Maybe I could also take one lunch away from my desk, even if it is only 15 minutes.
What might make that lunch more likely?
I can ask a coworker to walk with me.
That way I am less likely to turn it into an errand or stay inside answering emails.
That is a thoughtful use of connection.
What are you taking from today?
That asking for something clearly is not the same as being needy.
I still do not like it.
But I am starting to see that silence has a cost too.
That is a strong place to end.
You have been practicing direct requests with Nora, your sister, and your supervisor.
What have you learned about the moments before you ask?
I start negotiating against myself.
I decide what the other person probably has going on.
Then I decide my need is not important enough to interrupt it.
What information do you have when you make that decision?
Usually none, I am guessing.
I know that, but it still feels polite.
There's a difference between considering another person and making the whole decision for them without letting them respond.
That is exactly what I do.
I call it being considerate, but it also means I never have to risk hearing no.
What would a respectful request sound like if the other person were free to say yes, no, or not now?
Do you have 10 minutes to talk this week?
It would mean a lot, but I understand if you do not.
That feels better than waiting for someone to notice.
It gives both people room to be honest.
I tried it with my sister.
We talked for 20 minutes and I did not have to pretend I was fine.
Afterward, I felt guilty for taking her time, but I also felt closer to her.
Which feeling stayed longer?
The closeness The guilt came back later when I was trying to sleep, but I could recognize it as the old voice.
What did you say back to the old voice?
I said, She chose to be there It was not magic, but it stopped me from sending an apology text at midnight.
That is a real shift.
You let the connection stand without immediately trying to cancel it out.
I think I do that at work too.
Someone helps me and then I feel like I have to repay them right away.
What happens when help is treated as a debt?
I become less likely to ask for it, or I say yes to something I do not have capacity for because I feel I owe people.
Is there a way to acknowledge help without turning it into a contract?
I could just say thank you.
I know that sounds obvious.
Obvious and difficult can coexist.
My supervisor helped me sort the launch tasks this week.
I thanked her and then I almost volunteered for another committee.
I stopped myself.
What helped you stop?
I asked whether I actually had time before I answered.
The answer was no.
I said I could not take it on this month.
She said, That makes sense.
Again, nobody was angry.
You are collecting evidence that a boundary can be ordinary rather than catastrophic.
I want that to become more believable than the worst case version.
What would help it become believable?
Keeping examples.
I could make a small note on my phone, requests made, response received, what actually happened.
Then when I am convinced everyone will be disappointed, I have something concrete to look at.
That is an excellent experiment for the launch period.
I will try it.
